translations.text: Now once more I will make known in words, through poetic skill and the mind's recollection, a song about a kind of fish: about the great whale.
He is often met, against their will, by seafarers and by everyone. He is dangerous and fierce of spirit. A name has been given to him, the floater on the ancient streams: Fastitocalon.

His appearance is like a rough stone, as if it were drifting by the water's shore, surrounded by sand-dunes, the greatest of sea-reeds [?], so that seafarers think they are looking at some island with their eyes,

and then they moor their high-prowed ships to that false land with anchor-ropes. They settle the sea-steeds at the water's edge, and then they go up onto that island, bold of heart. The ships stand fast by the shore, surrounded by the current.
Then the weary-hearted seafarers make camp, expecting no danger. On the island they kindle flame and light a high fire. The men are joyful, though worn out in spirit, and eager for rest.
Then the one skilled in deceit feels that the travellers are settled firmly on him, keeping their camp and enjoying the weather.
Then suddenly the ocean's spirit goes down with the ship into the salt wave and seeks the sea floor. Then, in the hall of death, he holds the ships and their crews fast in drowning.
Such is the custom of demons, the way of devils: as they go about their work, they use secret power to deceive the people and lure them into the ruin of their good deeds.
They lead them astray at will, so that the people seek support and comfort from enemies, until they firmly choose their dwelling there with the traitor.
When the treacherous, insolent enemy from the living torment recognizes that every one of the race of men is firmly fastened in his ring,
he then becomes their life-slayer through cruel cunning, to the proud and the humble alike, who here wickedly do his will. With them he suddenly [?]

Covered with a helmet of concealment and stripped of all good things, he seeks hell, the bottomless surge beneath the misty gloom, just like the great whale that sinks seafaring men and their wave-horses.
The proud rusher through the waters has another trait that is even more wondrous.
When hunger troubles him in the sea and the monster craves food, the guardian of the sea opens his mouth and his wide lips.
A pleasant scent comes from inside him, and by it other kinds of sea-fish are deceived. They swim swiftly to the place where the sweet scent comes out.
They go in there, an unwary crowd, until the wide jaw is filled. Then suddenly he claps his grim jaws together around the plunder.

So it is for every man who most often regards his life carelessly in this passing time. He lets himself be deceived by a sweet scent and false desire, so that he is stained with sins against the King of glory.
After their death-journey the accursed one opens hell to meet them, those who falsely and foolishly pursued the body's pleasure against the right counsel of the mind,
When the deceitful one, skilled in evil, has brought those who cling to him, covered in sins, into that fortress at the surging whirlpool,
[?] and who before, in the days of their life, eagerly obeyed his teachings, when after their death-agony he snaps his grim jaws firmly together, the barred door of hell.
those who come in there have no turning back, no escape, and never any way out, any more than the fish travelling the sea can turn back from the whale's grip.
Therefore it is in every way [?] the Lord of lords, and always renounce devils in words and deeds, so that we may see the King of glory.
Let us always seek peace and salvation from him in this fleeting time, so that we, with one so beloved, may enjoy glory in praise forever.
